sections.title: 1. Pastoral Economy & Livestock
sections.content:
Centrality of Pastoralism

The Rigvedic economy was predominantly pastoral and semi-nomadic. The primary source of livelihood and measure of wealth was livestock, specifically cattle (Gau). Society was cattle-centric, and ownership of large herds determined social status. A wealthy person was referred to as Gomat. Cattle were not only the chief form of property but also served as a medium of exchange and standard of value in trade.

Livestock Vocabulary and Significance

The supreme importance of cattle is reflected in the extensive cattle-based vocabulary in Rigvedic Sanskrit:

  • Gavisthi / Gaveshana: Literally meaning 'search for cows', these terms were used as synonyms for conflicts or warfare, indicating that battles were essentially cattle raids.
  • Gavyuti: A measure of distance, defined by how far a cow's bellow could be heard.
  • Godhuli: A measure of time (dusk/evening), denoting the hour when cattle returned from grazing.
  • Duhitr: The term for daughter, literally translating to 'one who milks cows', reflecting the division of pastoral labor in the household.

Other Domesticated Animals

Besides cows, the early Indo-Aryans domesticated several other animals. The horse (Ashva) was highly valued for military purposes, drawing war chariots (Rathas). Sheep (Avi), goats (Aja), dogs (used for herding and security), and oxen (used for transport) were also bred. The horse and the cow were the twin pillars of early Indo-Aryan mobility and subsistence.

sections.title: 2. Agriculture & Cultivation
sections.content:
Secondary Role of Tillage

Agriculture was a secondary occupation in the early Rig Vedic period, subservient to pastoralism. Because the clans were mobile and constantly migrating across the Sapta-Sindhu region, long-term settled cultivation was limited. Tillage was primarily subsistence-oriented, producing enough grains to supplement the dairy-centric diet.

Agricultural Tools and Terminology

Despite its secondary status, the Rigveda contains several references to agricultural operations and implements, especially in the later Mandalas:

  • Langala / Sira: The wooden plough share, drawn by oxen to turn the soil.
  • Sita: The furrow made by the plough, which was personified as a goddess of fertility in later hymns.
  • Khanitra: Shovels or digging tools used for manual excavation.
  • Yava: The principal grain cultivated, translating generally to barley. Rice (Vrihi) and wheat (Godhuma) were completely absent in the early parts of the Rigveda.

Farming Operations

Rigvedic hymns describe the basic cycle of farming, including sowing seeds, harvesting crops using sickles (Datra), threshing grain on the threshing floor (Khalya), and winnowing. Artificial irrigation was primitive, relying mainly on wells (Avata) and natural rain, with channels (Kulya) occasionally mentioned to divert river waters to fields.

sections.title: 3. Crafts, Metals & Industries
sections.content:
The Status of Artisans

In the Rigvedic economy, artisans and craftsmen were highly valued members of the tribe, enjoying respectable social standing and participating in popular assemblies. Since the economy was non-sedentary and required constant production of mobile equipment (weapons, wagons, clothes), crafts were essential for tribal survival.

Key Industrial Groups

The Rigveda mentions several specialized professional groups:

  • Takshan (Carpenter): Crafted wood items, particularly war chariots (Rathas) and transport wagons (Anas). Chariots were complex engineering marvels featuring spoked wheels, which gave the Aryans military dominance.
  • Karmara (Metalworker): Worked with metals to forge tools, domestic utensils, and weapons. The metal they worked with was called Ayas, which refers to copper or bronze. Iron (known later as Krishna-ayas) was not yet known or processed in early Vedic times.
  • Vayatri (Weaver): Primarily women, who engaged in spinning and weaving wool (extracted from sheep of the Gandhara region) and cotton to make clothing.
  • Charmakara (Leatherworker): Prepared leather for water bags, reins, bowstrings, and protective guards.

sections.title: 4. Trade, Barter & Currency
sections.content:
Barter as the Dominant Exchange System

The Rigvedic economy lacked regular commercial markets and minted coins. Trade was conducted entirely through the barter system, where goods were directly exchanged. The cow (Gau) was the ultimate unit of value, with prices of commodities (like images of gods or weapons) commonly quoted in cows.

Pre-Monetary Currency Tokens

Though coins were absent, certain valuable metal objects served as standard currency tokens in transaction systems:

  • Niska: A gold neck ornament or disc that came to represent a fixed weight of gold, acting as a transition towards metallic currency.
  • Rukma: A decorative gold plate worn on the chest, also used as a valuable token in gifts and high-value barter exchange.

The Panis

The merchant class or traders are referred to as Panis in the Rigveda. They were wealthy non-Aryans who hoarded cattle wealth and engaged in trade. The Panis were highly criticized in Vedic hymns because they did not perform sacrifices (Yajnas), did not give gifts (Dakshina) to priests, and were often accused of stealing the Aryan clans' cattle herds, leading to inter-tribal battles.

sections.title: 5. Taxation & Redistribution
sections.content:
The Voluntary Nature of Bali

In the early Rig Vedic period, there was no regular or compulsory tax system. The state structure was not yet developed enough to maintain a permanent revenue bureaucracy. The only form of tribute mentioned is Bali. During this pastoral phase, Bali was a voluntary offering or gift made by clansmen to the Rajan as a token of respect, loyalty, and in exchange for leadership and protection.

Redistribution of Spoils

The tribal economy relied heavily on war booty (including captured cattle, horses, grain, and chariot equipment) acquired during raids. The Rajan did not hoard this wealth. Instead, it was brought to the popular tribal assembly, the Vidatha, which functioned as the primary redistribution organ. The spoils were divided among the clansmen, priests (as Dakshina), and warriors according to custom, preventing extreme wealth concentration and maintaining the egalitarian fabric of the tribe.

sections.title: 6. Economic Transition & Settled Life
sections.content:
Eastward Migration and Agriculture

Towards the end of the Rig Vedic period (c. 1000 BCE), the Aryan tribes began migrating from the semi-arid Sapta-Sindhu region (Punjab/Haryana) towards the wetter Ganga-Yamuna Doab. This geographical shift coincided with a transition from a mobile pastoral economy to sedentary agriculture. The clearing of forests and clearing of fields led to the emergence of permanent cultivated land plots, designated in texts as Kshetra.

Emergence of Land Rights

While early Rigvedic pasture lands were communal, the transition to agriculture triggered the development of individual family claims over cultivated lands. The concept of private fields developed, though communal pasture ownership (Gavyuti) remained. The surplus generated from agriculture led to early class divisions, transforming voluntary Bali into compulsory taxation, paving the way for the territorial states of the Later Vedic era.

practiceQuestions.q:
With reference to the early Vedic economy, consider the following statements:
1. The cow (Gau) was the primary standard of value and medium of exchange.
2. Pastoralism was the dominant occupation, while agriculture played a secondary role.
3. Wealthy individuals were designated as 'Gomat'.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: All three statements are correct. Cows served as currency standard, pastoralism was primary, and cattle owners were called Gomat.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding agricultural practices in the Rigvedic period:
1. Barley (Yava) was the principal grain cultivated.
2. Deep tillage using heavy iron ploughshares was common.
3. The furrow made by a plough was referred to as 'Sita'.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Heavy iron ploughshares were unknown; wooden ploughs (Langala) were used since iron (Krishna-ayas) was not processed yet (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q:
With reference to the metal technology of the Rigvedic period, consider the following statements:
1. The term 'Ayas' was used to denote copper or bronze.
2. Weaponry and tools were made using iron technology.
3. Craftsmen like metalworkers (Karmaras) held a respectable social status.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Iron technology was absent; copper/bronze was used (Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the merchant group called 'Panis':
1. They were rich non-Aryans who hoarded cattle and traded commodities.
2. They were widely praised in Rigvedic hymns for their generous gifts to Purohitas.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Panis were hated by priests because they refused to perform sacrifices or offer gifts (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic political economy, what was the nature of 'Bali'?
opts: A voluntary offering made by clansmen to the Rajan as a token of loyalty
A mandatory tax on agricultural fields collected by the Rajan's bureaucracy
A transit tax collected at trade checkpoints by pasture officers
A fine imposed on clansmen who committed theft or cattle-lifting
practiceQuestions.sol: Bali was a voluntary gift or tribute given to the Rajan by his clansmen as respect and loyalty.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following assemblies in early Vedic polity was primarily responsible for the redistribution of war spoils and communal offerings?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Vidatha was the oldest tribal assembly which handled the ritual sharing and redistribution of booty.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to Rigvedic currency and exchange, which of the following is correct?
opts: Trade was dominated by barter, with gold ornaments like Niska serving as standard tokens
A well-organized metallic coinage system featuring copper coins was used
The state treasury issued silver bars stamped by the Rajan's seal
Foreign trade was conducted using cowry shells imported from Rome
practiceQuestions.sol: Barter was dominant, with gold neck ornaments (Niska) acting as value tokens. Minted coins were absent.

practiceQuestions.q:
Match the following Rigvedic professionals with their economic roles:
1. Takshan - A. Carpenter
2. Karmara - B. Metalworker
3. Charmakara - C. Leatherworker
4. Vayatri - D. Weaver
Choose the correct code:
practiceQuestions.sol: Takshan is Carpenter, Karmara is Metalworker, Charmakara is Leatherworker, Vayatri is Weaver.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the late Rigvedic economic transition?
opts: Migration to the Ganga valley led to settled agriculture and emergence of private land plots (Kshetra)
Aryan clans returned to Central Asia due to agricultural failures
The state established a heavy corporate monopoly over artisanal guilds
Gold coins completely replaced the barter system in local village transactions
practiceQuestions.sol: Eastward migration to the wetter Ganga valley facilitated permanent farming and the emergence of individual fields (Kshetra).

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the status of land ownership in the early Rigvedic period:
1. Private individual ownership of land was the foundation of wealth.
2. Pasture lands were held communally by the clan (Vis or Jana).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 2 is correct. In the early pastoral phase, pastures were communal; individual private titles did not exist (so Statement 1 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Gavyuti' in the Rigvedic texts was used to denote:
opts: The title of a pasture officer
practiceQuestions.sol: Gavyuti was a measure of distance, literally how far a cow's bellow could be heard, showing cattle-centric life.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following is correct regarding the Rigvedic term 'Godhuli'?
practiceQuestions.sol: Godhuli refers to dusk, the time when cattle return from grazing, highlighting the pastoral time measurement.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the division of labor in the early Vedic family, the term 'Duhitr' (daughter) literally means:
practiceQuestions.sol: Duhitr literally translates to 'one who milks cows', reflecting how pastoral labor was divided in the Kula.

practiceQuestions.q:

1. The horse-drawn chariot (Ratha) and wooden cart (Anas) were the main vehicles.
2. Maritime trade across distant oceans was highly organized with royal navies.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Chariots and carts were standard. Distant sea trade did not exist; early Vedic trade was localized barter, so Statement 2 is false.

practiceQuestions.q: The crop designation 'Vrihi' in Vedic literature represents rice. When does Vrihi appear as a dominant cultivated crop?
practiceQuestions.sol: Rice (Vrihi) became dominant in Later Vedic times; early Rigvedic relied mostly on barley (Yava).

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic economy, what was the primary source of raw wool used by weavers to make garments?
opts: Flax fibers harvested in Punjab valleys
practiceQuestions.sol: Wool was extracted from sheep, and Gandhara sheep were famous for high-quality wool (Urna).

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the division of spoils, which assembly oversaw the allocation of boot under the supervision of the Rajan?
practiceQuestions.sol: The oldest assembly Vidatha distributed resources, ensuring communal equality and support for priests.

2. Grains were ground using mortar and pestles and stone mills.

practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Dairy products were staples, and grinding barley with stone mills was common.

practiceQuestions.q: What was the term used in the Rigvedic agricultural context to denote the wooden plough share?
practiceQuestions.sol: Langala (or Sira) was the term for the wooden plough share used to till agricultural fields.

practiceQuestions.q: In the early Vedic period, the term 'Adhivasa' refers to which of the following?
opts: An outer cloak or garment draped over the shoulders
practiceQuestions.sol: The Adhivasa (or Atka) was an outer drape or cloak worn over the standard Vasa garment.

practiceQuestions.q:
Assertion (A): Rigvedic economy was highly dependent on raids and warfare.
Reason (R): Chieftains acquired cattle herds, horses, and wagons by raiding neighbor clans.
Codes:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
practiceQuestions.sol: Raids (Gavisthi) were a core economic activity to acquire cattle wealth, which was then distributed in assemblies.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the early Vedic crafts and technology:
1. Spoked-wheel chariots (Rathas) were constructed by Takshans.
2. Potters manufactured red and black pottery for domestic storage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Carpenters made spoked-wheel Rathas, and potters produced standard domestic wares.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic trade layout, the standard barter value of an image of Indra or a weapon was typically calculated in terms of:
practiceQuestions.sol: Commodity values were assessed in cows, which was the standard unit of value.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the status of the 'Karmara' in Rigvedic economic administration?
opts: A metalworker who produced copper and bronze weapons and tools
A tax collector who managed the distribution of agricultural taxes
A merchant leader of the non-Aryan trade guild
The head of the royal treasury in charge of distributing booty
practiceQuestions.sol: The Karmara was a metalworker who forged tools and weapons from copper/bronze (Ayas).

practiceQuestions.q:
Assertion (A): Rigvedic clans did not construct monumental brick structures or cities.
Reason (R): Their mobile pastoral life and lack of agricultural surplus limited sedentary cities.
Codes:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
practiceQuestions.sol: Nomadic pastoralism and lack of sedentary farming surplus meant there was no base for brick cities or permanent urbanization.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the Later Vedic transitions, the transition from voluntary 'Bali' to compulsory taxes was driven by:
opts: Settled agriculture producing surplus wealth and territorial state formation
Royal decrees issued by the Roman empire during trade contacts
The direct commands of the Purohitas in the Upanishads
A severe drought that destroyed all pastoral cattle herds
practiceQuestions.sol: Settled farming created food surplus and territorial claims, enabling chiefs to enforce regular taxes (Bhaga) instead of voluntary gifts.

practiceQuestions.q: In the context of Rigvedic farming, what does the term 'Datra' refer to?
opts: A sickle used to harvest crops
practiceQuestions.sol: Datra refers to the sickle used for harvesting mature grains like barley.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the economic resources in Rigvedic times:
1. Forests were used communally for hunting and timber collection.
2. Mines were operated by the central state treasury to mint gold coins.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Forests were common resource areas. Mines and state treasuries did not exist; there was no coinage system (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following professional crafts was primarily dominated by women (Vayatri) in Rigvedic economic setup?
practiceQuestions.sol: Weaving and spinning (textiles) was a domestic craft primarily managed by women weavers (Vayatri).

practiceQuestions.q: What was the term used in late Rigvedic texts to denote the settled villages that developed from kin camps?
practiceQuestions.sol: Grama evolved from a mobile kin camp (during migration) into a permanent sedentary village layout.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the division of wealth in early Vedic society:
1. The spoils of war were divided among priests, warriors, and clansmen.
2. The Rajan held a private warehouse of grain and cattle that was strictly non-distributable.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Booty was redistributed in Vidatha; the Rajan did not hoard private non-distributable warehouses (so Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic pastoral economy, what was the primary source of milk curd and butter (ghee)?
practiceQuestions.sol: Cows were the primary dairy source, providing ghee, butter, and curd for daily consumption and rituals.

practiceQuestions.q: The gold neck ornament 'Niska' is often described as a value standard. With reference to Niska, which statement is correct?
opts: It was a gold ornament of a standard weight that transitioned to a currency token
It was a copper coin stamped by local merchants
It was a weapon used in chariot battles
It was a ritual tool used to measure pasture boundaries
practiceQuestions.sol: Niska was a gold necklace/ornament of a fixed weight, serving as a pre-monetary currency token.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding early Vedic craft integration:
1. The production of leather (for reins and bowstrings) was carried out by Charmakaras.
2. Artisans were restricted to hereditary guilds that regulated prices.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Charmakaras made leather products. Hereditary guilds and rigid price controls did not exist (Statement 2 is false).

practiceQuestions.q: The crop term 'Yava' in Rigvedic hymns represents which agricultural crop?
practiceQuestions.sol: Yava was the standard Sanskrit term for barley, the chief grain cultivated.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the role of the 'Vis' (common people) in supporting the Rajan's political economy?
opts: Offering voluntary gifts (Bali) and fighting as local tribal militias in cattle raids
Paying mandatory land revenue taxes checked by Royal surveyors
Working as enslaved agricultural laborers on state farms
Providing professional silver currency to the treasury
practiceQuestions.sol: The Vis offered voluntary gifts (Bali) and fought in tribal militias during conflicts, as there was no professional army.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to the Later Vedic transition, the transition from copper/bronze tools to iron tools led to:
opts: Heavier tillage and forest clearing in the Ganga plain, facilitating settled farming
The complete decline of farming in favor of horse breeding
The establishment of central maritime trade routes with Rome
The dissolution of the Varna system
practiceQuestions.sol: Iron technology facilitated clearing of dense forests and heavy tillage in the Ganga plain, shifting the economy to agriculture.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the professional guilds in the early Rigvedic period:
1. Artisans like carpenters (Takshans) and weavers were respected members of the tribe.
2. A highly complex guild system with hereditary membership and laws was present.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct. Artisans were respected and sat in councils. Rigid hereditary guilds only developed in Later Vedic and classical times, so Statement 2 is false.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic period, the mobile camp or fighting unit of pastoral families was called the:
practiceQuestions.sol: The Grama was a mobile camp or marching unit of kin families led by the Gramani.

practiceQuestions.q:
Assertion (A): Rigvedic economy lacked regular commercial markets and money.
Reason (R): Trade was localized and conducted through barter, with cows as the standard of value.
Codes:
opts: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct, and the barter system explains the lack of formal commercial markets and coinage.

practiceQuestions.q: The term 'Avata' in the Rigvedic agricultural context refers to:
opts: A well used for drinking water and irrigation
practiceQuestions.sol: Avata refers to a well dug for water storage and basic irrigation of crops.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the term 'Kulya' in Rigvedic farming?
practiceQuestions.sol: Kulya refers to irrigation channels or canals used to divert river water to fields.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Rigvedic metalwork:
1. Metalworkers (Karmaras) worked copper and bronze into tools.
2. Potters manufactured Ochre Colored Pottery (OCP) for storage.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Karmaras forged copper/bronze, and OCP was the characteristic pottery of the period.

practiceQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic pastoral economy, the term 'Avi' refers to which domesticated animal?
practiceQuestions.sol: Avi is the Sanskrit word for sheep, bred for meat and wool.

practiceQuestions.q: What was the term used in the Rigvedic period for the threshing floor where harvested barley was processed?
practiceQuestions.sol: Khalya (or Khala) represents the threshing floor where grain was separated from chaff.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the term 'Anas' in Rigvedic transport?
opts: A heavy draft cart pulled by oxen
A merchant boat used for river travel
A leather harness for war horses
practiceQuestions.sol: Anas was a heavy transport cart or wagon pulled by oxen, used for carrying family goods during migration.

practiceQuestions.q: With reference to early Vedic exchange systems, the gold plate ornament 'Rukma' was traditionally used as a:
opts: Valuable currency token in high-value barter transactions
Crown worn by the Purohita during rituals
practiceQuestions.sol: Rukma was a valuable gold chest plate used as a currency token in high-value barter and gifts.

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the tax collection in Later Vedic times compared to the Rigvedic period:
1. The office of Bhagadugha (tax collector) was created to collect mandatory taxes.
2. Taxes were paid in the form of grain and cattle.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. In Later Vedic times, Bhagadugha was appointed, and taxes were collected in kind (grain and cattle).

practiceQuestions.q: The Sanskrit term 'Aja' in Rigvedic economic vocabulary refers to which animal?
practiceQuestions.sol: Aja is the Sanskrit word for goat, which was bred for milk and meat.

practiceQuestions.q: Which of the following represents the primary agricultural tool used to manually clear weeds and dig soil in the Rigvedic period?
practiceQuestions.sol: The Khanitra was a digging shovel used for manual weed clearing and digging soil.

mockTestQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic economic layout, who were the 'Panis'?
opts: Wealthy non-Aryan merchants who hoarded cattle and refused sacrifices
The head priests of the tribal assemblies
The carpenters who built spoked-wheel chariots
The tax collectors appointed by the Rajan
mockTestQuestions.sol: Panis were wealthy non-Aryan traders criticized for hoarding cattle and refusing to support Vedic sacrifices.

mockTestQuestions.q: What does the term 'Gomat' refer to in the Rigvedic society?
opts: A wealthy individual possessing large herds of cattle
The military commander of the infantry
The assembly elder in charge of judicial disputes
A title of the Purohita during sacrifices
mockTestQuestions.sol: Gomat literally translates to 'one who owns cows', representing a rich person.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following grains was the chief agricultural crop cultivated in the early Rigvedic period?
mockTestQuestions.sol: Yava (barley) was the primary grain cultivated; rice and wheat appeared in Later Vedic times.

mockTestQuestions.q: The metal referred to as 'Ayas' in the early Rigvedic hymns represents:
mockTestQuestions.sol: Ayas in early Vedic texts refers to copper or bronze tools/weapons; iron was discovered later.

mockTestQuestions.q: The tribute called 'Bali' offered by clansmen to the Rajan in the early Vedic period was characterized as:
opts: A voluntary offering reflecting loyalty and respect
A mandatory tax on cultivated land
A commercial fee on trade checkpoints
A penalty fine for administrative crimes
mockTestQuestions.sol: Bali was a voluntary gift or tribute given to the Rajan, without any formal tax collection machinery.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which assembly acted as the central organ for distributing war spoils and communal offerings in Rigvedic times?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The oldest tribal assembly Vidatha was responsible for resource redistribution and sharing of war booty.

mockTestQuestions.q: What was the pre-monetary gold necklace currency token used in early Vedic trade?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Niska was a gold neck ornament of a standard weight that served as a value standard in barter.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which professional craftsman was responsible for building spoked-wheel war chariots (Rathas)?
mockTestQuestions.sol: The Takshan (carpenter) held a respected position because of his engineering role in making chariots.

mockTestQuestions.q: In the Rigvedic agricultural context, what does the term 'Sita' represent?
opts: The furrow made by a plough
mockTestQuestions.sol: Sita represents the furrow made by the plough, which was personified as a goddess of fertility.

mockTestQuestions.q: Which of the following describes the status of land ownership in the early Rigvedic period?
opts: Pasture land was communal property of the clan, and private titles did not exist
The Rajan had absolute private ownership of all land plots
Individual families registered private land titles with priests
Agricultural fields were owned exclusively by women
mockTestQuestions.sol: Pastures and fields were held collectively by the clan; private land ownership was not established in this phase.

items.phrase: G-Y-A-N (Gau: cow wealth, Yava: barley, Ayas: copper, Niska: gold necklace)
items.decryption: Remember: GYAN covers the core Rig Vedic economic items (Gau, Yava, Ayas, Niska).

traps.title: UPSC Common Exam Traps to Avoid
items: Trap: Iron ploughshares were used to clear forests in early Rigvedic times. **False.** Iron (Krishna-ayas) only appeared at the very end of the period (c. 1000 BCE). Copper/bronze (Ayas) was used in early phases.
Trap: The Rajan collected mandatory land revenue during the pastoral phase. **False.** Chieftains had no revenue officers; Bali was a voluntary tribute, and redistribution occurred in assemblies.
